Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
Going out at night or being outside after dark

issues.item: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
issues.explanation: These three maladaptive strategy items do not form a clinically coherent set on their own. 'Avoid Dreams' and 'Avoid Physical Stress' are trauma-linked avoidance strategies, but 'Compulsive Cleaning' reflects a distinct control/ritualising pattern that is not clearly tied to the same military PTSD presentation in the absence of any supporting trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items. With no active edges in the formulation, the node should still be internally coherent; here the items suggest different mechanisms (nightmare avoidance, bodily arousal avoidance, and compulsive control rituals) without evidence they belong to the same symptom pattern.

vignette:
Yasmin

Yasmin was twenty-two months removed from the IED strike that killed two of her fellow soldiers and left her with a shattered tibia, a surgical scar that still ached in cold weather, and a conviction that her body had become a liability she could no longer trust. She had been a junior enlisted database administrator with the Army Corps of Engineers, stationed in Kandahar, when the convoy she was riding in hit the roadside bomb. The blast threw her against the interior wall of the Humvee; she remembered the sound first-not the explosion itself, which her mind had somehow skipped over, but the metallic shriek of the vehicle's frame buckling and the wet, urgent sounds of her colleagues. She remembered the smell of burning plastic and fuel, and the way her left leg had gone numb before the pain arrived in waves so severe that she'd bitten through the inside of her cheek. The combat medic had told her later that she'd stopped breathing for a moment, and that her body had seized up so completely they'd had to manually straighten her leg to get her on the stretcher.

For the first few months after her medical discharge and return to civilian life in Dearborn, Michigan, Yasmin had assumed the hypervigilance and the nightmares were simply what recovery looked like. She had thrown herself into her new job at a healthcare IT firm, grateful for the structure and the quiet of the server room. But as autumn turned to winter, she had begun to notice that her body felt like a trap. Any situation that made her heart race-rushing to meet a deadline, climbing stairs, even the anxiety of a video call with her supervisor-sent her into a state of dread so complete that she would talk herself out of the activity entirely. She had stopped going to the gym, stopped walking to the coffee shop near the office, stopped accepting her colleague Ravi's invitations to after-work dinners because the prospect of sitting in a restaurant where she couldn't control the exits and where her pulse might quicken made her feel like she was failing some crucial test of her own stability.

What had truly begun to unravel her life, though, was the cleaning. It had started small-a need to wipe down her desk at the end of each workday, to organize her files in a very particular way. But over the months, the ritual had metastasized into something that consumed her evenings. She would come home from work and spend two or three hours scrubbing her apartment, reorganizing her kitchen cabinets, laundering her clothes, vacuuming the same carpet over and over. Her hands had become raw and cracked. She had called in sick to work twice because she'd lost track of time during a cleaning cycle and had only realized at 11 p.m. that she hadn't slept. Her mother, Fatima, had begun to worry aloud about the chemical smell that now seemed to emanate from Yasmin's bedroom, and had gently suggested that perhaps this was not normal. Yasmin knew it wasn't normal. But when she tried to stop, when she sat down at 6 p.m. with the intention of simply eating dinner and watching television, the feeling of chaos and contamination would rise in her chest until she couldn't bear it anymore, and she would be on her feet, gloves on, spray bottle in hand.

The darkness had become its own separate prison. Yasmin had not been outside after sunset in nearly four months. She had arranged her work schedule so that she arrived before dawn and left by 4:30 p.m., and she had begun to make excuses to avoid any social obligation that might require her to be out when the light failed. She told herself it was about visibility, about being able to see threats. But truthfully, the night felt like the moment when her body might betray her again, when she might lose control in a space where no one could help her.

It was her supervisor's gentle but direct feedback-that her productivity had declined and that she'd become isolated from her team-that had finally cracked through Yasmin's private calculus of survival. She sat in the intake session with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her eyes fixed on the floor, and said quietly: "I don't know how to live like this anymore. I don't know how to trust myself."
